doc.title: Bobby Shew interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 1, 2020

title: Dalton Smith's chop exercise; Carnival of Venice and keeping ego out
summary: Shew passes a double-tongue part to Warren Luening, and explains passing parts to colleagues such as Nelson Hatt and avoiding ego.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: It pays for a lot of Aleves and Advils. But you know I have to tell you one time I was doing a thing at Universal and the trumpet section you know it’s a funny thing that Dalton Smith, who was a great guy to play with and work with all the time, Stan Kenton’s lead player for a while. But sometimes they used to write stuff so high and ridiculously hard for me, I’d finish it and I’d get it done but I’d go Christ why do they write like this for me and oh my God, you know? And Dalton said you know one time, he said, “There’s an exercise that you can do,” he said, “and if you do that exercise it saves your chops and you can last forever.” And I said, “Really? I need to know what is that exercise?” He says, “Here, you play this and you play that.”
Oh that’s a good one. You don’t find — they don’t teach you that in music school.

No they don’t. So I was doing a thing at Universal Studios one day and it was just sort of like a silly movie about like the late 20s or early 30s or something. And it was a scene where there was a little kind of a John Philip Sousa tiny band on a gazebo in a park and people were all walking through on a Sunday afternoon you know, and they’re dressed up and all of that. And you turn the page and there’s “Carnival of Venice.” What? Why the writer had to put that there. He could have put anything there, but this was, somebody said, “Oh I’m going to put ‘Carnival of Venice.’” So it’s like you must hate trumpet players you know, to make, all of a sudden you turn the page and there’s this thing. Well I couldn’t play that thing ever in my life. Not now and not then. Because I never took any lessons as a kid, I never learned to double tongue or triple tongue. I had no classical training whatsoever you know, other than playing marches in my high school band, that was it. You know and other than that I was just a jazz guy and a big band person. So I played on some salsa bands but I couldn’t double tongue. So you know I looked at that thing and there’s Warren Luening sitting right next to me and I went, “You got it.” And Warren had done all of that. He had done all that stuff and I just passed the part to him and he nailed it just like the old Del Staigers one. And it was not the entire thing but it was enough that I couldn’t have played it, not in a million years. Well when we did the “Tony Randall Show” the theme, the first session is a piccolo trumpet. What the hell? Nelson Hatt. Here you go, Nelson. So you pass the part. Because you’ve got to keep — one of the things is that it’s very important in those situations is you cannot go in there with an ego issue. You’re asking for trouble if you do. Because ego is really simply defined as self-importance. When you’re important and I have to do this, and I’m going to brag about ‘cause I did this. Well you’re going to shit all over that piccolo trumpet part and everybody on the planet is going to know who sucked on that piccolo thing on the “Tony Randall Show.” “Oh that was Shew.” I shoulda figured. But you should know when to say no. Shew passed the part to Nelson Hatt. Oh that Shew is a smart cookie. And so you’ve got to keep your ego completely out of the picture when you go into those
